"title": "Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4",
"authors": "Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych; Caue Ribeiro",
"field_subfield": "Materials chemistry / agricultural science (green chemistry, reverse logistics)",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental study (materials synthesis and nutrient-release characterization)",
"executive_summary": "This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry. The authors propose a free-solvent mechanochemical process that combines eggshell waste (a food-industry residue rich in calcite, CaCO3) with monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4) to synthesize new phosphate phases, principally K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, aimed at improving the management of phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and calcium (Ca) in soil systems. The central hypothesis is that these mechanochemically derived phosphates act as 'smart release' fertilizers: they delay the bioavailability of the highly soluble P and K (which release rapidly from KH2PO4) while simultaneously enhancing the bioavailability of Ca, which is otherwise extremely slow to release from eggshell CaCO3. The mechanochemical activation is performed in a solvent-free environment using a high-energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette 7), with the goal of minimizing waste and energy consumption while promoting solid-phase ion migration and new structure formation. The experimental design systematically varied milling time (15 min to 24 h) and milling speed (100 to 600 rpm) to evaluate the acid-base reactions between the precursors. Characterization was performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR MAS), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), with nutrient content determined by acid digestion followed by atomic absorption and colorimetric methods. Nutrient release behavior was evaluated in two complementary systems: a citric acid solution (2 wt%) following the MAPA recommended procedure, and soil-based release essays (both diffusion-zone visualization and aerobic soil conditions). The key results demonstrate that the milled samples exhibit slower release of P and K compared to the KH2PO4 precursor, while showing faster Ca release compared to the eggshell CaCO3 precursor. In soil, the 2 h/600 rpm sample showed a progressive P release reaching 45 mg/kg after 30 days (15% of total P), intermediate radial diffusion (34% faster than struvite, 22% slower than KH2PO4), and increased bioavailable Ca reaching 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days (~8% recovery). The formation of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) was identified in soil conditions from 3 to 30 days, explaining the slower release trend. The study concludes that this mechanochemical approach yields an eco-friendly fertilizer that guarantees better nutrient management by playing on the solubility of Ca, K, and P, with no unwanted subproducts and no solvent waste. The work contributes to the current socio-environmental scenario by prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products, avoiding unnecessary economic losses. A notable limitation is that the study did not report specific quantitative release rates or kinetic constants for all nutrients, and the bibliography appears to be omitted, which limits the ability to fully assess the theoretical foundations and reproducibility of the work. The absence of reported details such as the exact train/test analogs (here, precursor vs. milled samples), randomization of sample preparation, and complete characterization parameters in the main text also represents a gap, though the Supplementary Material is referenced for additional details. Overall, the study provides a reproducible framework for producing smart-release fertilizers from eggshell waste, with clear implications for sustainable agriculture and waste valorization.",

{
"title": "Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4",
"authors": "Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro",
"field_subfield": "Materials chemistry / agricultural chemistry (reverse logistics, mechanochemistry, fertilizer science)",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental research article (materials synthesis, characterization, and release kinetics)",
"executive_summary": "This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry. The authors propose a free-solvent mechanochemical process that combines eggshell waste (calcite, CaCO3) with monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4) to synthesize new phosphate phases, primarily K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4. These phases are classified as smart release fertilizers because they delay the bioavailability of phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) while improving the bioavailability of calcium (Ca). The mechanochemical process occurs in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste and ensuring significant savings during production. The study demonstrates that the synthesized phosphates exhibit slower release kinetics for P and K compared to the precursor KH2PO4, while showing faster release of Ca compared to the precursor eggshell (CaCO3). This behavior is attributed to the formation of potassium calcium phosphate phases and, subsequently, hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) under soil conditions. The research is grounded in the concept of reverse logistics, which emphasizes the collection and reuse of solid waste, and the application of solid-state mechanochemical activation to promote chemical reactions from solid reagents using mechanical energy. The findings suggest that the produced materials could be an excellent alternative for nutrient management in soils, particularly those with a pH around 5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. The study also highlights the importance of new technologies of ecological fertilizer production that prioritize environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products, avoiding unnecessary economic losses. Overall, the research contributes to the development of eco-friendly fertilizers that can improve soil conditioning and nutrient management while reducing environmental impact and economic costs.",

{ "The reverse logistic is perfectly applied in the agriculture context, providing novel processes for the synthesis of different calcium and/or potassium phosphates from any source of calcium carbonate.": "perfectly applied in the agriculture context" },
{ "Eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite).": "excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite)" },
{ "Everyday millions of tons of eggshells are produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth.": "millions of tons of eggshells...disposed in landfills" },
{ "Solid-state mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy to promote a chemical reaction from solid reagents using mainly friction and impact forces.": "applying mechanical energy to promote a chemical reaction" },
{ "The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca.": "classified as smart release fertilizers" },
{ "The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process.": "reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment" },
{ "No mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate (K3CaH(PO4)2) and potassium calcium phosphate (CaKPO4) from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4.": "no mechanochemical process has been reported" },
{ "New technologies of ecological fertilizer production have been prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products.": "prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes" }

"research_question_and_hypothesis": [
{ "The central research question is whether a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 can produce new potassium calcium phosphate phases with improved nutrient management.": "whether a free-solvent mechanochemical process...can produce new potassium calcium phosphate phases" },
{ "The hypothesis is that the synthesized phosphates (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4) will exhibit slower release of P and K compared to the precursor KH2PO4, while showing faster release of Ca compared to the precursor eggshell (CaCO3).": "the synthesized phosphates...will exhibit slower release of P and K" },
{ "The predicted outcome is that these materials will act as smart release fertilizers, delaying the bioavailability of P and K while improving the bioavailability of Ca, thus improving nutrient management in soil systems.": "these materials will act as smart release fertilizers" },
{ "It is hypothesized that the formation of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) under soil conditions will further contribute to the slow release of Ca and P, making these materials an excellent alternative for long-term nutrient management.": "the formation of hydroxyapatite...will further contribute to the slow release" },
{ "The study predicts that the mechanochemical process will occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste and ensuring huge savings during the production process.": "the mechanochemical process will occur in a solvent-free environment" },
{ "The authors predict that the new phosphate phases will provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca, turning these materials an excellent alternative in nutrient management.": "the new phosphate phases will provide a delay of the bioavailability" },
{ "The study hypothesizes that the solubility of the phosphates will be influenced by the size of the metal cation and its charge, influencing the reticular energy of the structure.": "the solubility of the phosphates will be influenced by the size of the metal cation" },
{ "The authors predict that the produced materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability.": "the produced materials would promote better nutrient management" }
],
"methodological_details": [
{ "The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process.": "collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water" },
{ "The KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec.": "The KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec" },
{ "The milling process was performed with a high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter.": "high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl" },
{ "The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, firstly for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h.": "weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w)...at 600 rpm...at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h" },
{ "Considering the purity of KH2PO4 and assuming that the eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3.": "the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3" },
{ "After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance, magic-angle spinning (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).": "characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance...TGA, and DSC" },
{ "The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods.": "acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C)" },
{ "Before release essays at citric acid solution (2 wt%), the material has been pelletized to simulate commercial products.": "Before release essays at citric acid solution (2 wt%), the material has been pelletized" },
{ "The pellets were obtained in a steel pelletizer applying the pressure of 5 bar, and the weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P.": "applying the pressure of 5 bar, and the weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P" },
{ "One single pellet was used in each essay in triplicate, placed in a 10 mL beaker, immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, kept closed with PVC film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring.": "One single pellet...in triplicate...in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring" },
{ "Aliquots of 1.2 mL at different times (from 15 min to 30 days) were collected to evaluate the release behavior and allow the calculation of a release kinetic model of Ca, K and P.": "Aliquots of 1.2 mL at different times (from 15 min to 30 days) were collected" },
{ "The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014).": "The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes...according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014)" },
{ "In each Petri dish with a diameter of 8.6 cm, 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil were added to achieve the desired density of 1.2 g.cm-3.": "In each Petri dish with a diameter of 8.6 cm, 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil" },
{ "In order to achieve 70% of the maximum soil water retention capacity, 15 mL deionized water were added.": "In order to achieve 70% of the maximum soil water retention capacity, 15 mL deionized water were added" },
{ "The papers are scanned and analyzed using image software (GNU Image Manipulation Program, v. 2.6.11, Free Software).": "The papers are scanned and analyzed using image software (GNU Image Manipulation Program, v. 2.6.11)" },
{ "Soil release essays were carried out under aerobic conditions in a plastic container containing 50 g of sandy soil with 75% water saturation.": "Soil release essays were carried out under aerobic conditions in a plastic container containing 50 g of sandy soil" },
{ "The experiments were performed at 3, 7, 15 and 30 days, using a single pellet for each container, the pellet weight was standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil.": "The experiments were performed at 3, 7, 15 and 30 days...the pellet weight was standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil" },
{ "Potassium and calcium were extracted from the soil by HCl (0.05 Mol/L) and KCl (1 Mol/L) methods, respectively; and phosphorus was extracted from soil using Mehlich 1 method (Embrapa, 1979).": "Potassium and calcium were extracted from the soil by HCl (0.05 Mol/L) and KCl (1 Mol/L) methods" },
{ "A colorimetric analysis of molybdenum blue was used to quantify phosphorus released content into the solution (Murphy and Riley, 1962) and potassium and calcium released content were quantified by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (FAAS), with a PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T instrument.": "A colorimetric analysis of molybdenum blue was used to quantify phosphorus released content" },
{ "The XRD 6000 diffractometer (Shimadzu) was used to obtain X-ray diffraction patterns, with a Cu Kα incident beam (λ = 0.1546 nm) and scanning speed of 2° min-1 at 30 kV voltage and 40 mA current.": "The XRD 6000 diffractometer (Shimadzu) was used...with a Cu Kα incident beam (λ = 0.1546 nm)" },
{ "The 31P NMR MAS analysis was carried out using an Avance III HD / Bruker equipment, with the sample rotated at 10KHz, using the sequence HPDEC and the chemical shift reference was ADP with phosphate line at 0.8 ppm.": "The 31P NMR MAS analysis was carried out using an Avance III HD / Bruker equipment" }

"key_results": [
{ "The milling process between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm produced a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4.": "The milling process between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm produced a mixture of phosphates" },
{ "Below these milling parameters (time and milling speed) only the reactants diffraction patterns are found, i.e., no evidence of chemical reaction is observed.": "Below these milling parameters...only the reactants diffraction patterns are found" },
{ "There is a direct relationship between the time and milling speed and the increasing of total energy involved.": "There is a direct relationship between the time and milling speed and the increasing of total energy involved" },
{ "In general, it was noticed that only a minimal energy is required to initiate the mechanochemical reaction, and as a consequence, the diffraction patterns have huge changes attributed to the formation of different polymorphic potassium calcium phosphate phases.": "only a minimal energy is required to initiate the mechanochemical reaction" },
{ "When milling time increases, secondary reactions begin, for example, mechanochemical dehydroxylation of the new formed phosphates.": "When milling time increases, secondary reactions begin, for example, mechanochemical dehydroxylation" },
{ "The TGA curve of KH2PO4 shows two main loss events: the first step at 200°C should be associated to crystallization water loss, and the second step at 300°C corresponds to polycondensation, concomitant with structural water loss.": "The TGA curve of KH2PO4 shows two main loss events: the first step at 200°C...the second step at 300°C" },
{ "The residual mass (89%) regards to KPO3 formation is consistent to the theoretical (87%).": "The residual mass (89%) regards to KPO3 formation is consistent to the theoretical (87%)" },
{ "The thermal degradation of eggshell has two main steps: a first mass loss step below 300 °C attributed to moisture elimination concomitant with organic membrane degradation; and a second step related to calcite decomposition below 700 °C.": "The thermal degradation of eggshell has two main steps: a first mass loss step below 300 °C...a second step related to calcite decomposition below 700 °C" },
{ "In the case of milled samples, three mass loss events are observed: the first step, centered at 280°C, is related to crystallization water loss; the second step, centered at 420°C, is associated to partial structural water loss and structure dimerization; and the final step, centered at 710°C corresponds to final structural water loss reaction and structure polycondensation.": "In the case of milled samples, three mass loss events are observed: the first step, centered at 280°C...the second step, centered at 420°C...the final step, centered at 710°C" },
{ "All the samples milled at 600 rpm do not present calcite decomposition below 700 °C, but in the samples milled for 2 h at 400 rpm this event is still observed.": "All the samples milled at 600 rpm do not present calcite decomposition below 700 °C" },
{ "It suggests that in low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite to form calcium potassium phosphates.": "It suggests that in low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite" },
{ "The 31P NMR MAS spectra of the precursor KH2PO4 shows a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm, characteristic of monosubstituted phosphate.": "The 31P NMR MAS spectra of the precursor KH2PO4 shows a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm" },
{ "The shift at δ = 3.28 ppm (2 and 6 h at 600 rpm) and at δ = 2.82 ppm (24 h at 600 rpm) are reported to calcium phosphates compounds, for example, hydroxyapatite and octocalcium phosphate.": "The shift at δ = 3.28 ppm (2 and 6 h at 600 rpm) and at δ = 2.82 ppm (24 h at 600 rpm) are reported to calcium phosphates compounds" },
{ "The signal at δ = 0.74 ppm is related to disubstituted phosphate, suggesting H(PO4)2 5-species agreeing with the KCaPO4 formation.": "The signal at δ = 0.74 ppm is related to disubstituted phosphate, suggesting H(PO4)2 5-species" },
{ "A shift was also observed at around δ = -5 ppm (marked at δ = -4,78 ppm) in sample milled by 2 h at 600 rpm, attributed to pyrophosphate formed by phosphate dimerization.": "A shift was also observed at around δ = -5 ppm (marked at δ = -4,78 ppm) in sample milled by 2 h at 600 rpm" },
{ "The kinetic study of the nutrient release was firstly evaluated in citric acid solution (wt 2%) according to the recommended procedure from MAPA to analyze fertilizer solubility.": "The kinetic study of the nutrient release was firstly evaluated in citric acid solution (wt 2%) according to the recommended procedure from MAPA" },
{ "Phosphorus and potassium release behavior were similar for the precursor (KH2PO4) and milled samples, but slower for milled samples, this fact shows that the phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management maintaining their bioavailability.": "Phosphorus and potassium release behavior were similar for the precursor (KH2PO4) and milled samples, but slower for milled samples" },
{ "Calcium release is rather different for eggshell to the milled samples. Even that CaCO3 in the eggshell may be soluble in acids, the kinetic was extremely slow in comparison, evidencing the solubility of phosphates formed.": "Calcium release is rather different for eggshell to the milled samples...the kinetic was extremely slow in comparison" },
{ "Phosphorus and potassium presented better correlation with pseudo-second order model, considering 'R 2 ' and the values related to concentration at equilibrium time 'qe' and 'experimental qe' (Table 1 ).": "Phosphorus and potassium presented better correlation with pseudo-second order model, considering 'R 2 '" },
{ "For both nutrients there was a substantial decrease of the kinetic constant from KH2PO4 to milled samples, attesting the delay in nutrient supply after mechanochemical processing and certainly related to the formation of potassium calcium phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4).": "For both nutrients there was a substantial decrease of the kinetic constant from KH2PO4 to milled samples" },
{ "Even not possible to compare kinetic constants for the calcium release, it is important to highlight that in this case was observed an opposite effect: the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available.": "Even not possible to compare kinetic constants for the calcium release...the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available" },
{ "The temporal profile for the precursor KH2PO4 indicates a P increase from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg after 3 days of release keeping constant after 30 days, representing 40% of total P from precursor (KH2PO4).": "The temporal profile for the precursor KH2PO4 indicates a P increase from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg after 3 days of release" },
{ "For sample 2 h/600 rpm, the phosphorus release is more progressive (from 0 mg/kg to 25 mg/kg at 3 days and 45 mg/kg at 30 days) corresponding to 15% of total P content recovered from the milled sample.": "For sample 2 h/600 rpm, the phosphorus release is more progressive (from 0 mg/kg to 25 mg/kg at 3 days and 45 mg/kg at 30 days)" },
{ "These results indicate that sample 2 h/600 rpm presented a longer delay in phosphorus release compared to the precursor (KH2PO4), corroborating with the results observed in citric acid solution.": "These results indicate that sample 2 h/600 rpm presented a longer delay in phosphorus release compared to the precursor (KH2PO4)" },
{ "At day 2 it is possible to see that struvite was not able to release any phosphorus, while sample 2h/600rpm the P diffusion reach a value of 1.99 cm a significant value compared to 2.62 cm for KH2PO4, a source of P considered extremely soluble.": "At day 2 it is possible to see that struvite was not able to release any phosphorus, while sample 2h/600rpm the P diffusion reach a value of 1.99 cm" },
{ "After 30 days, struvite starts P delivery, but sample 2h/600 rpm has a control release keeping lower values compared to KH2PO4.": "After 30 days, struvite starts P delivery, but sample 2h/600 rpm has a control release keeping lower values compared to KH2PO4" },
{ "Results showed that the P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor at the end of 30 days.": "Results showed that the P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor" },
{ "There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied in soil, but this concentration increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery from sample (Fig. 6 ).": "There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied in soil, but this concentration increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days" },
{ "These results corroborate with citric acid solution release essays and attest efficient use of 2 h/600 rpm sample as a source of bioavailable calcium compared to the precursor eggshell -CaCO3.": "These results corroborate with citric acid solution release essays and attest efficient use of 2 h/600 rpm sample as a source of bioavailable calcium" },
{ "The slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation -(Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) -identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions (Fig. 7 ).": "The slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation" },
{ "In an additional experiment, samples ground at 600 rpm were suspended in water, dried and then characterized by XRD, in which the phase transition to Hydroxyapatite was observed for all of them (Fig. S5 ).": "In an additional experiment, samples ground at 600 rpm were suspended in water, dried and then characterized by XRD" },
{ "Hydroxyapatite is an important long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer, turning systematically soluble by the natural soil pH acidification, especially under pH 5.": "Hydroxyapatite is an important long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer, turning systematically soluble by the natural soil pH acidification" }

"interpretation_and_theoretical_implications": [
{ "The study demonstrates that the synthesized potassium calcium phosphates (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4) act as smart release fertilizers, delaying the bioavailability of P and K while improving the bioavailability of Ca.": "The study demonstrates that the synthesized potassium calcium phosphates act as smart release fertilizers" },
{ "The slower release of P and K compared to the precursor KH2PO4 is attributed to the formation of potassium calcium phosphate phases, which delay the nutrient supply.": "The slower release of P and K compared to the precursor KH2PO4 is attributed to the formation of potassium calcium phosphate phases" },
{ "The faster release of Ca compared to the precursor eggshell (CaCO3) is attributed to the solubility of the phosphates formed, which release Ca more readily.": "The faster release of Ca compared to the precursor eggshell (CaCO3) is attributed to the solubility of the phosphates formed" },
{ "The formation of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) under soil conditions further contributes to the slow release of Ca and P, making these materials an excellent alternative for long-term nutrient management.": "The formation of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) under soil conditions further contributes to the slow release of Ca and P" },
{ "The study highlights the importance of the mechanochemical process, which occurs in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste and ensuring huge savings during the production process.": "The study highlights the importance of the mechanochemical process, which occurs in a solvent-free environment" },
{ "The results suggest that the produced materials could be an excellent alternative for nutrient management in soils, particularly those with a pH around 5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils.": "The results suggest that the produced materials could be an excellent alternative for nutrient management in soils" },
{ "The study contributes to the development of new technologies of ecological fertilizer production that prioritize environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products.": "The study contributes to the development of new technologies of ecological fertilizer production that prioritize environmental care" },
{ "The findings support the concept of reverse logistics, which emphasizes the collection and reuse of solid waste, and the application of solid-state mechanochemical activation to promote chemical reactions from solid reagents.": "The findings support the concept of reverse logistics, which emphasizes the collection and reuse of solid waste" },
{ "The study demonstrates that the mechanochemical process can be used to produce new phosphate phases with improved nutrient management, playing on the solubility of calcium, potassium and phosphorus.": "The study demonstrates that the mechanochemical process can be used to produce new phosphate phases with improved nutrient management" },
{ "The results indicate that the produced materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability.": "The results indicate that the produced materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium" }

{
"title": "Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4",
"authors": "Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro",
"field_subfield": "Materials chemistry / agricultural science",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental study",
"executive_summary": "This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry principles. The authors propose a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste (calcite) and KH2PO4 to synthesize new phosphate phases, namely K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, which provide better nutrient management of phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and calcium (Ca) when applied to soil systems. The material first releases K and forms hydroxyapatite, serving as an important P and Ca bioavailable source at pH ~5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. The research context emphasizes that reverse logistics is one of the most important instruments for applying shared responsibility for the product lifecycle, and eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite). The methodological approach involved collecting eggshells from the authors' homes, washing them with water, drying at room temperature, and grinding using a high-energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette 7) with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The milling process was performed using a weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, first for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h, and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400, and 600 rpm for 2 h. The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milling, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content was obtained by dissolving the samples using acid digestion in an H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. The release essays were performed in citric acid solution (2 wt%), where the material was pelletized to simulate commercial products, with the pellets obtained in a steel pelletizer applying a pressure of 5 bar and the weight standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet was used in each essay in triplicate, placed in a 10 mL beaker immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, kept closed with PVC film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014), with each Petri dish having a diameter of 8.6 cm and 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil to achieve a density of 1.2 g/cm³. The key results show that the milling process between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm produces a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4. Below these milling parameters, only the reactants' diffraction patterns are found, indicating no evidence of chemical reaction. The TGA curve of KH2PO4 shows two main loss events: the first step at 200°C associated with crystallization water loss, and the second step at 300°C corresponding to polycondensation concomitant with structural water loss. The residual mass (89%) regarding KPO3 formation is consistent with the theoretical (87%). The thermal degradation of eggshell has two main steps: a first mass loss step below 300°C attributed to moisture elimination concomitant with organic membrane degradation, and a second step related to calcite decomposition below 700°C. For milled samples, three mass loss events are observed: the first step centered at 280°C related to crystallization water loss, the second step centered at 420°C associated with partial structural water loss and structure dimerization, and the final step centered at 710°C corresponding to final structural water loss reaction and structure polycondensation. The 31P NMR MAS spectra of the precursor KH2PO4 shows a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm, characteristic of monosubstituted phosphate. The shift at δ = 3.28 ppm (2 and 6 h at 600 rpm) and at δ = 2.82 ppm (24 h at 600 rpm) are reported to calcium phosphates compounds, and the signal at δ = 0.74 ppm is related to disubstituted phosphate, suggesting H(PO4)2 5-species agreeing with the KCaPO4 formation. The kinetic study of the nutrient release was firstly evaluated in citric acid solution (2 wt%), and phosphorus and potassium release behavior were similar for the precursor (KH2PO4) and milled samples, but slower for milled samples, showing that the phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management maintaining their bioavailability. For both nutrients, there was a substantial decrease of the kinetic constant from KH2PO4 to milled samples, attesting the delay in nutrient supply after mechanochemical processing. The temporal profile for the precursor KH2PO4 indicates a P increase from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg after 3 days of release, keeping constant after 30 days, representing 40% of total P from precursor. Differently, for sample 2 h/600 rpm, the phosphorus release is more progressive (from 0 mg/kg to 25 mg/kg at 3 days and 45 mg/kg at 30 days) corresponding to 15% of total P content recovered from the milled sample. The P radial diffusion for the sample 2h/600rpm in soil reached a value of 1.99 cm, a significant value compared to 2.62 cm for KH2PO4, and struvite was not able to release any phosphorus at day 2. Results showed that the P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor at the end of 30 days. There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied in soil, but this concentration increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery from sample. The interpretation and theoretical implications suggest that the slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation, identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions. Hydroxyapatite is an important long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer, turning systematically soluble by the natural soil pH acidification, especially under pH 5. The contradictions and limitations include the fact that below the milling parameters (time and milling speed), only the reactants' diffraction patterns are found, indicating no evidence of chemical reaction, and that all samples milled at 600 rpm do not present calcite decomposition below 700°C, but in samples milled for 2 h at 400 rpm this event is still observed, suggesting that low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite. The claims supported by evidence indicate that the mechanochemical process produces new phosphate phases such as K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4, which present a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The data and code availability is not reported, as the details of each characterization are described in Supplementary Material, and the soil properties are presented in Table S1. The robustness and ablation notes indicate that the milling process was performed to evaluate acid-basic reactions between the precursors to form potassium calcium phosphates. The ethical considerations are not explicitly reported, but the study is based on reverse logistics and green chemistry, using eggshell, a food industry residue, and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer. The key figures and tables include Figure 1 showing the XRD patterns of the powders obtained after milling, Figure 2 showing the TGA curves, Figure 3 showing the calcined samples, Figure 4 showing the 31P NMR MAS spectra, Figure 5 showing the nutrient release behavior in citric acid solution, Figure 6 showing the nutrient release behavior in soil, and Figure 7 showing the hydroxyapatite formation. The top influential citations include Tibben and Lembke (2002), Byeon (2016), Kouznetsov et al. (2016), Jenkins et al. (1999), and Liu and Lal (2015). The three takeaways are: (1) the core contribution is the development of an eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell and KH2PO4 using a free-solvent mechanochemical process; (2) the strongest evidence is the demonstration that the new phosphate phases delay the bioavailability of P and K while increasing the Ca bioavailability; (3) the future path is the use of the sample 2h/600rpm as nanocomposites to promote better solubilization of P and Ca when faster release is required. "
}

summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro
summary.field_subfield: Materials chemistry / green chemistry / agricultural science
summary.executive_summary: This study develops an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, using a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4. The research is grounded in reverse logistics, which the authors describe as an important instrument for applying shared responsibility for the products lifecycle. Eggshells are highlighted as important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite). The milling process was performed with a high-energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette 7), with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using a weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, milled for various durations (15 min to 24 h) and at various speeds (100 to 600 rpm). The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milling, samples were characterized by XRD, NMR MAS, TGA, and DSC. Nutrient content was obtained by acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Release essays were conducted in citric acid solution (2 wt%) and in soil (Petri dishes with 78 g of dry soil, 1.2 g.cm^-3 density, 70% water retention). The results indicate that the milling process produces new phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4), which present a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. In soil essays, the concentration of bioavailable calcium increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for the 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery. The P radial diffusion for the 2h/600 rpm sample is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than the precursor at the end of 30 days. The authors conclude that these materials promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The study is based on reverse logistic and green chemistry, using eggshell, a food industry residue, and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer. The results indicate new phosphate phases that present slower release of potassium and phosphorus in citric acid solution, and faster release compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The soil essays indicate the same behavior, but with a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution essays, explained by hydroxyapatite formation, which is an important source of calcium and phosphorus as a long-term slow release fertilizer.

claims.description: A free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 can produce calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning.
The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study develops an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, using a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4. The research is grounded in reverse logistics, which the authors describe as an important instrument for applying shared responsibility for the products lifecycle. Eggshells are highlighted as important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite). The milling process was performed with a high-energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette 7), with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using a weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, milled for various durations (15 min to 24 h) and at various speeds (100 to 600 rpm). The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milling, samples were characterized by XRD, NMR MAS, TGA, and DSC. Nutrient content was obtained by acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Release essays were conducted in citric acid solution (2 wt%) and in soil (Petri dishes with 78 g of dry soil, 1.2 g.cm^-3 density, 70% water retention). The results indicate that the milling process produces new phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4), which present a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. In soil essays, the concentration of bioavailable calcium increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for the 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery. The P radial diffusion for the 2h/600 rpm sample is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than the precursor at the end of 30 days. The authors conclude that these materials promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The study is based on reverse logistic and green chemistry, using eggshell, a food industry residue, and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer. The results indicate new phosphate phases that present slower release of potassium and phosphorus in citric acid solution, and faster release compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The soil essays indicate the same behavior, but with a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution essays, explained by hydroxyapatite formation, which is an important source of calcium and phosphorus as a long-term slow release fertilizer.

Research Context
Reverse logistics is considered one of most important instruments for applying shared responsibility for the products lifecycle. Reverse logistics is an instrument of economic and social development characterized by a set of actions, procedures and means to enable the collection and restitution of solid waste to the business sector, for reuse, in its cycle or in other cycles productive, or other environmentally appropriate final destination (Tibben and Lembke, 2002). The reverse logistic is perfectly applied in the agriculture context. Eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite) (Byeon, 2016). Everyday millions of tons of eggshells are produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth. The literature reports the mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) from different precursors to those reported in this study (Chaikina et al., 2019). As far as the authors know, no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate (K3CaH(PO4)2) and potassium calcium phosphate (CaKPO4) from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4. New technologies of ecological fertilizer production have been prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products (Ivanov et al., 2019; Krishna et al., 2017; Santos et al., 2019; Cichy et al., 2019).

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 can produce calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning. The study hypothesizes that the K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 phases formed provide a better nutrient management of P, K and Ca, when applied in soil system the material first release K and form hydroxyapatite and important P and Ca bioavailable source at pH ~ 5. The study hypothesizes that the produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. The study hypothesizes that the solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process, ensuring huge savings during the production process. The predicted outcome is that these materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The predicted outcome is that the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available, an opposite effect to the delay in nutrient supply for phosphorus and potassium.

Methodological Details
The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process. The KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec. The milling process was performed with high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, milled for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h. Considering the purity of KH2PO4 and assuming that the eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance, magic-angle spinning (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Before release essays at citric acid solution (2 wt%), the material has been pelletized to simulated commercial products. The pellets were obtained in steel pelletizer applying the pressure of 5 bar, and the weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet was used in each essay in triplicate, placed in 10 mL beaker, immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, kept closed with PVC film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014). In each Petri dish with diameter of 8.6 cm, 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil were added to achieve the desired density of 1.2 g.cm^-3.

Procedures And Architectures
The milling process was performed with high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, milled for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h. Considering the purity of KH2PO4 and assuming that the eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance, magic-angle spinning (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. The pellets were obtained in steel pelletizer applying the pressure of 5 bar, and the weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet was used in each essay in triplicate, placed in 10 mL beaker, immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, kept closed with PVC film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014). In each Petri dish with diameter of 8.6 cm, 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil were added to achieve the desired density of 1.2 g.cm^-3. In order to achieve 70% of the maximum soil water retention capacity, 15 mL deionized water were added. The papers are scanned and analyzed using image software (GNU Image Manipulation Program, v. 2.6.11, Free Software). The scanned images are converted to black-with binary images, using a threshold color value (e.g. on a 0-255 scale), and the area of the high P-zone is quantified using the histogram command.

Key Results
The milling process between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm produce a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF database n° 22-1218) and possibly CaKPO4 (PDF database n° 33-1002). Bellow these milling parameters (time and milling speed) only the reactants diffraction patterns are found, i.e., no evidence of chemical reaction is observed. There is a direct relationship between the time and milling speed and the increasing of total energy involved. In general, it was noticed that only a minimal energy is required to initiate the mechanochemical reaction, and as a consequence, the diffraction patterns have huge changes attributed to the formation of different polymorphic potassium calcium phosphate phases. When milling time increases, secondary reactions begin, for example, mechanochemical dehydroxylation of the new formed phosphates. The TGA curve of KH2PO4 shows two main loss events: since it is an anhydrous material, the moisture loss is not seen and the first step at 200°C should be associated to crystallization water loss. The second step at 300°C corresponds to polycondensation, concomitant with structural water loss. The residual mass (89%) regards to KPO3 formation is consistent to the theoretical (87%). The thermal degradation of eggshell has two main steps: a first mass loss step below 300 °C attributed to moisture elimination concomitant with organic membrane degradation; and a second step related to calcite decomposition below 700 °C. The eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, as attested by XRD pattern, which is also confirmed by the small difference from experimental residue (56%) and the theoretical (59%). In the case of milled samples, three mass loss events are observed: the first step, centered at 280°C, is related to crystallization water loss; the second step, centered at 420°C, is associated to partial structural water loss and structure dimerization; and the final step, centered at 710°C corresponds to final structural water loss reaction and structure polycondensation. All the samples milled at 600 rpm do not present calcite decomposition below 700 °C, but in the samples milled for 2 h at 400 rpm this event is still observed. It suggests that in low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite to form calcium potassium phosphates. The 31 P NMR MAS spectra of the precursor KH2PO4 shows a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm, characteristic of monosubstituted phosphate. The shift at δ = 3.28 ppm (2 and 6 h at 600 rpm) and at δ = 2.82 ppm (24 h at 600 rpm) are reported to calcium phosphates compounds.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results indicate that the phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management maintaining their bioavailability, as phosphorus and potassium release behavior were similar for the precursor (KH2PO4) and milled samples, but slower for milled samples. The new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available, an opposite effect to the delay in nutrient supply for phosphorus and potassium. Considering the kinetic behavior, it was observed that these materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The results indicate that sample 2 h/600 rpm presented a longer delay in phosphorus release compared to the precursor (KH2PO4), corroborating with the results observed in citric acid solution. The P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor at the end of 30 days. The slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation, identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions. Hydroxyapatite is an important long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer, turning systematically soluble by the natural soil pH acidification, especially under pH 5.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study notes that even not possible to compare kinetic constants for the calcium release, it is important to highlight that in this case was observed an opposite effect: the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available. The study notes that in low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite to form calcium potassium phosphates. The study notes that for milling during 2 h at 600 rpm, this sample has an unclear phosphate phase, but after thermal treatment at 280 °C it slightly changes matching with K3CaH(PO4)2 phase. The study notes that the soil essays indicate the same behavior, but a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution essays, this can be explained by hydroxyapatite formation. The study notes that the authors collected the eggshells in their homes, which may introduce variability in the composition of the eggshells. The study notes that the details of each characterization are described in Supplementary Material, which may not be fully accessible.

The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process. Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study notes that the essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, milled for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h, in order to evaluate acid-basic reactions between these precursors. The study notes that all the samples milled at 600 rpm present a similar thermal decomposition, but with different residuals masses according to the milling time. The study notes that in an additional experiment, samples ground at 600 rpm were suspended in water, dried and then characterized by XRD, in which the phase transition to Hydroxyapatite was observed for all of them.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the XRD patterns of the powders obtained after milling, indicating the formation of K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF database n° 22-1218) and possibly CaKPO4 (PDF database n° 33-1002). Figure 2 shows the TGA curves of the samples, indicating the thermal degradation events. Figure 3 shows the calcined samples, indicating the phase transitions. Figure 4 shows the 31 P NMR MAS spectra of the precursor KH2PO4 and milled samples. Figure 5 shows the kinetic study of the nutrient release in citric acid solution (wt 2%). Figure 6 shows the kinetic study of the nutrient release in soil. Table 1 shows the kinetic constants for the nutrient release. Table S1 shows the nutrient content of the samples and precursors. Table S2 shows the chemical and physical soil properties.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of an eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell waste and KH2PO4 using a free-solvent mechanochemical process. 2. The strongest evidence is the production of new phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4) that present slower release of potassium and phosphorus and faster release of calcium compared to the precursors. 3. The future path is the use of the sample 2h/600rpm as nanocomposites to promote better solubilization of P and Ca if faster release is required.
